title: TB7-24192
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of China, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his/her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of China, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his/her claim for refugee protection. The Appellant asks that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) and substitute a decision with its own determination that the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. In the alternative, the Appellant requests that the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD with a differently constituted panel. The Appellant has submitted new evidence with the appeal as referred to in subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA), and he does not request an oral hearing be held, pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.
Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD and dismisses the appeal.

The Appellant alleged before the RPD that he was born in Akollegalaling, Tibet. He states that his date of birth is XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX He alleges that he left Tibet and travelled to Dharamsala in India. He attended the Tibetan Children's Village School for four or five years and then began working in a restaurant kitchen, and he finally became a restaurant cook. He has a Registered Foreigner's Certificate (RC) that was given to him by the Indian government. He states that he does not have the right to apply for Indian citizenship because he was born in Tibet and that he is at risk of being deported back to Tibet from India.

With assistance from an agent/smuggler, he obtained a fraudulent Indian passport. Using the passport, the Appellant applied for a Canadian visa in August of 2016. He traveled from New Delhi to Toronto, and in March of 2017, he filed his claim for refugee protection. The Appellant's hearing for refugee protection was held on May 1, 2017 and September 18, 2017. In a decision on October 23, 2017, the RPD rejected the Appellant's claim finding that the Appellant had not established his identity. The Appellant submits that the interpretation at the hearing was flawed and that the RPD erred in drawing its credibility findings and in its treatment of the documentary evidence.

For questions of fact, law, and mixed fact and law, I have applied the standard of correctness, as per Huruglica. In assessing issues involving credibility of oral testimony, I may apply the RAD modified standard of reasonableness in those situations where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage, as per the decision in X (Re), 2017 CanLII 33034 (CA IRB). ADMISSIBILITY OF NEW EVIDENCE PRESENTED ON APPEAL
In support of this appeal, the Appellant submitted an affidavit from an interpreter, a partial transcript of the hearing and the interpreter's analysis of the segments from the partial transcript.2

Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the Appellant may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected3 in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection. It is for the appellants to make full and detailed submissions in their Memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) and how that evidence relates to the appellants.4

In addition, if the new evidence meets one of the explicit legislative factors in subsection 110(4), then the second step of the analysis is for the RAD to apply the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh.5 In Singh, the Federal Court of Appeal held that the RAD should assess the admissibility of the new evidence for its credibility, relevance and newness. The RAD is not to consider the fourth Raza factor of materiality to the admission of new evidence, which is a consideration for subsection 110(6) and the request for an oral hearing.6

The Appellant submits that the proposed new evidence meets the test of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA because it arose after the issuing of a decision in his claim before the RPD. The Affidavit and Partial Transcript

The RAD notes, in its review of the new evidence, that it arose following the rejection of the Appellant's claim by the RPD. The RAD notes that the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh7 set out that the RAD should further assess the admissibility of the new evidence for its credibility, relevance and newness. The RAD has reviewed the interpreter's affidavit, the partial transcript, the audio recording of the hearing as well as the record.

The RAD notes that the affiant states that he is fluent in both the Tibetan and English languages, but there is a statement that he is not a certified interpreter. Nonetheless, the RAD will assess the affiant's submissions.

The Federal Court, in Mohammadian, stated: Perfect translation is not required as translation is an inherently human endeavour which often takes place in less than ideal circumstances. The goal is linguistic understanding.8

The RAD notes that the function of an interpreter at an RPD hearing is to provide interpretation assistance and not exact translation. The Federal Court, in Basyony, stated in paragraph 8 of the decision: Some errors in translation, which do not affect the overall outcome of the hearing, are not sufficient for that conclusion [that the hearing is defective]. One is mindful of the fact that translation is not an exact science. There is always room for differences in nuance between what is said in one language and its translation into another.9

The test for the adequacy of interpretation during a refugee determination hearing has recently been reiterated by the Federal Court in Jovinda v Canada (IRCC): 27. The foundation of translation adequacy was set out by the Supreme Court of Canada in R v Tran, 1994 CanLII 56 (SCC), [1994] 2 SCR 951, which was applied by the Federal Court of Appeal in Mohammadian v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2001 FCA 191 (CanLII) with respect to immigration matters. In Mohammadian, the Court stated that "the interpretation provided to applicants before the Refugee Division must be continuous, precise, competent, impartial and contemporaneous." This Court elaborated on the requirements of translation in that translation need not be perfect when performed at a hearing where contemporaneous translation is required, it must, however, be adequate (Bouanga v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 1029 (CanLII); Singh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 1161 (CanLII)).10

The RAD notes that the affiant has submitted an "audit report",11 which details specific errors in interpretation through the course of the RPD hearing. The RAD has reviewed these errors and considered their applicability and relevance to the findings of the RPD in arriving at its decision in this claim. The RAD has listened to the audio recording of the hearing and reviewed the partial transcript of the RPD hearing. The RAD finds that, despite some variance in terminology, most of the information identified as problem areas in the "audit" was interpreted in a format that allowed the Appellant to respond in a manner that confirmed that he fully understood the information being put to him. For example, at item three of the "audit report" taken from the second sitting: At 36:39, the member asked: Did you consider asking your mother to outline in her statement that she searched for your RC, that you were not born in India and that you don't have citizenship there? The Interpreter translated: Can your mother write a letter saying that she searched for your RC at home, you were not born in India and that you don't have citizenship there?12

In a similar manner: At 38:19, the claimant stated: I have presented my Green Book, which I thought was sufficient to prove the point. The interpreter translated: I thought that since I have presented my original Green Book, I thought that would work.13

The RAD finds the Appellant's answer-that he did not request that his mother do that because he did not realize-was directly responsive to the RPD's inquiry, which confirms that the question was understood by the Appellant, despite an alleged variance in the terminology. The RPD subsequently asked the Appellant to explain why he did not make the request from his mother when he was well aware that his national identity was an issue. The RAD finds the response translated by the interpreter sufficiently relates to the response by the Appellant.

The RAD further notes: At 57:48, counsel for the Appellant asks: You indicated that you had one Green Book. Do you mean you have one now, or did you ever have any other one before this one? The interpreter translates: You indicated that you had one Green Book. Do you mean you have one Green Book, or did you mean you used to have one earlier, and this one is a continuation?14

The Appellant's testimony in response, which was not provided in the transcript sample, "I only remember having this booklet, before that I don't remember", again clearly confirms that the Appellant understood the question put to him.

The RAD finds the author of the affidavit has provided selective portions of questions and testimony from the RPD hearing, but these samples are not necessarily representative of the full interaction at the time. The RAD notes that, often in interpretation, there are terms or expressions in other languages or dialects which may not be directly transferable or interchangeable with the English language terminology.

The RAD further notes in areas where there seemed to be some confusion as to the response of the Appellant, the RPD appears alert and subsequently rephrased or refocused the inquiry. For example, at 15:01 of the second sitting of the hearing, the RPD is discussing the placement of the Canadian visa in the Appellant's Indian passport. The RPD senses that the Appellant has not understood the question put to him, as noted in the Appellant's partial transcript audit report. The RPD subsequently rephrases the question and obtains a response that addresses the question put to him.

The RAD finds, in its review of the audio recording as well as the partial transcript of the RPD hearing, that the affiant in the "audit report" has not necessarily provided a full and accurate reporting of the alleged translation errors during the hearing. On initial review, the RAD notes the errors appear to be numerous and potentially compromising. Yet, upon full assessment, the errors do not corrupt the issues being addressed nor do they directly impact the findings in the Appellant's claim.
The RAD notes that the Federal Court has stated that translation need not be perfect, but it must be adequate.

The RAD notes that, in order to be admitted as new evidence under the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh,15 the evidence must meet the requirements of credibility, relevance and newness. The RAD finds that the Appellant's new evidence does not meet the requirement of relevancy, in that it is not capable of demonstrating that the interpretation in the RPD hearing was not adequate. The RAD will not admit the Appellant's new evidence in this appeal.

The RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in subsection 110(3) of the IRPA that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal, is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim, and, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.16

The affidavit from an interpreter as well as the partial transcript of the hearing was not accepted as new evidence by the RAD. The requirements of subsection 110(6) of the IRPA have not been met, and the RAD has no discretion to hold a hearing based on this evidence.
The Appellant submits that there was a violation of natural justice when the Appellant was denied his right to competent interpretation. The RAD is not persuaded by the argument of the Appellant.
paragraphs.heading_before: ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL

paragraphs.text: The RAD has reviewed the Appellant's arguments with respect to the quality and accuracy of the interpretation in the section on new evidence and found it provided no persuasive evidence to confirm that the interpretation at the RPD hearing was not adequate. The RAD finds, in its review, that the RPD member was mindful of the quality of the interpretation at the hearing from the outset and took steps to ensure that both the interpreter and the Appellant understood and were provided opportunities to correct statements they did not understand. The RAD notes that interpreters and claimants/appellants are usually knowledgeable with respect to the information pertaining to the claim; yet, sometimes the RPD/RAD members and counsel look at aspects of a claim in a way that the claimant/appellant and the interpreter may not understand.

The RAD finds that these types of issues are a normal consequence in hearings where an interpreter is utilized. The RAD as well as RPD members are trained to be aware that appellants can be nervous, that variations in dialect exist; as well, understanding local or colloquial terminology may present difficulties in relating all of the information pertaining to their claim. The RAD finds, on its review of all of the evidence, that the RPD provided a fair and balanced hearing environment that ensured interpretation was continuous, precise, competent, impartial and contemporaneous. The RAD finds that there was no violation of natural justice, and the Appellant has not been denied his right to competent interpretation. The RAD finds the Appellant's argument fails. Identity

The RPD found the Appellant's civil and national identity was not established, on a balance of probabilities, in terms of his: name, date of birth, place of birth, country of birth and country(ies) of citizenship. The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in rejecting the Appellant's supporting documents such as his "Green Book", the letters from the lawyer and his mother. The RAD is not persuaded by the argument of the Appellant. Uncontested findings The Indian Passport

The RPD found: (a) It was not credible that the Appellant would not know the name of the individual he engaged to acquire a fraudulent Indian passport. (b) The Appellant's explanation that he destroyed the passport that he used to travel and enter Canada because it would be of "no use" to him was not credible. (c) The Appellant's explanation that he did not attempt to obtain a valid travel document from Indian authorities before resorting to obtaining a fraudulent passport was indicative of a willingness to mislead authorities. (d) That the Appellant's testimony that it would be "easier" to obtain a false passport and thereby run the risk of detection and apprehension by the very authorities he alleges could deport him back to Tibet is not credible. (e) The Appellant successfully used his allegedly fraudulent passport to apply for a Canadian visa, exit India and enter Canada without any difficulty. (f) The copy of the biodata page of the Appellant's passport submitted in evidence contained no visible improprieties or evidence of fraud.

When assessing this evidence as a whole, the RPD found that the Appellant's evidence with respect to his travel from India, utilizing his Indian passport and Canadian visa, did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Indian passport he used to travel to Canada was false or obtained fraudulently.

The RAD is mindful of the Federal Court's decision in Rasheed,17 which asserts that the basic rule in Canadian law is that foreign documents (whether they establish the identity or not of a claimant) purporting to be issued by a competent foreign public official should be accepted as evidence of their content unless the Board has some valid reason to doubt their authenticity.

The RAD takes notice of the comments of the Federal Court, in Mijatovic:18 [26] The Board is entitled to assume that a refugee claimant is a citizen of a country whose passport he or she holds. This presumption, however, can be rebutted. If there is evidence to indicate that a refugee claimant is not in fact a national of the country which issued the passport, the Board must consider the implications of such evidence. In Radic, Justice William P. McKeown noted that the Board is expected to be aware of concepts such as the use of passports of convenience. In Adrar, 1997 CanLII 16800 (FC), [1997] F.C.J. No. 695, Justice Bud Cullen quoted from Radic as follows: 14. The case law on the legal significance of passports is as follows. A passport is prima facie evidence of citizenship [Varin v. Cormier 1937 CanLII 344 (QC CS), [1937] 3 D.L.R. 588 (Que. S.C.)]. In Radic v. M.E.I. (1994), 85 F.T.R. 65 at p. 67, Mr. Justice McKeown wrote: Concerning the fact that the applicant had a passport from the new Yugoslavia; the Board is an expert Board and should be aware of the issue of passports of convenience. The Board made no reference to section 93 of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees Handbook on procedures and criteria for determining refugee status (re- edited Geneva, January 1992) at page 22 paragraph 93. The paragraph reads as follows: 93. Nationality may be proved by the possession of a national passport. Possession of such a passport creates a prima facie presumption that the holder is a national of the country of issue, unless the passport itself states otherwise. A person holding a passport showing him to be a national of the issuing country, but who claims that he does not possess that country's nationality, must substantiate his claim, for example, by showing that the passport is a so-called "passport of convenience" (an apparently regular national passport that is sometimes issued by a national authority to non-nationals). However, a mere assertion by the holder that the passport was issued to him as a matter of convenience for travel purposes only is not sufficient to rebut the presumption of nationality. In certain cases, it might be possible to obtain information from the authority that issued the passport. If such information cannot be obtained, or cannot be obtained within reasonable time, the examiner will have to decide on the credibility of the applicant's assertion in weighing all other elements of his story.

In essence, the passport is evidence of citizenship unless its validity is contested. The onus is then on the applicant to prove that the applicant is of a different citizenship than that indicated in the passport. The RAD finds the Appellant has not displaced that onus. The RAD has reviewed the findings of the RPD and finds they are without error. The Registration Certificate

The RPD found the Appellant's testimony about why he carried a partial copy of his RC card with him to Canada while allegedly utilizing a fraudulent passport was not credible. The Appellant testified that he was unaware of how he had obtained the RC document and that he thought the document was in India, but his mother could not locate the document. The Appellant subsequently provided a copy of his full RC document as a post-hearing disclosure. The RPD considered his inconsistent testimony in respect of the document and assigned the copy of the document little evidentiary weight. The RAD has reviewed the document. The RAD notes that, because the RC document is a copy and not an original, the RAD is unable to ascertain whether the document contains any security features and whether it is a genuine document. The RAD places little evidentiary weight on the copy of the RC document and further finds it is insufficient to prove identity or citizenship. The RAD finds the Appellant's failure to disclose his original RC card seriously undermines the Appellant's allegations that he is a Tibetan citizen born in China. The RAD has reviewed the findings of the RPD regarding this issue and finds they are without error. Letters Provided by XXXX XXXX and the Tibetan Children's Village

The RPD found the letters provided little persuasive evidence in support of the date and location of the Appellant's birth or his current citizenship. The RAD has reviewed the finding of the RPD regarding this issue and finds it is without error. Oral Testimony Regarding Childhood in Tibet, including Language Spoken

The RPD found the Appellant's inability to provide any meaningful details or description of his surroundings, neighbours, neighbouring villages and the like is, more likely than not, an indication that he was not born in Tibet and lived there until the age of eleven. The Appellant's ability to speak the Tibetan language was not sufficient to establish his place and date of birth, nor his current country(ies) of citizenship. The RAD has reviewed the finding of the RPD regarding this issue and finds it is without error. The Green Book and the Tibetan Refugee Transit Centre (TRTC) Letter

The RPD found the Appellant's testimony about how he obtained his letter from the TRTC19 in order to obtain his Green Book was inconsistent with the date of issue on the documents and detracted from his credibility. The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in rejecting the Green Book because he could not recall when he or his father obtained the document. The RAD is not persuaded by the argument of the Appellant.

The RAD has reviewed the audio recording as well as the record in this issue. The RAD notes that the Appellant was asked about the TRTC letter by the RPD. The Appellant's testimony was vague. He stated that the document had been issued "later on", "it's been a few years I don't recall exactly when". When asked what steps were taken to obtain the document, he subsequently explained that one of his relatives went to Nepal to obtain the document. He further testified that they had to provide a copy of his Green Book in order to get the letter. He testified that his Green Book was issued in 1995. The RPD noted for the Appellant that the letter from the TRTC was issued after the Green Book, which was contrary to his testimony. The Appellant responded that he did not recall when the Green Book was issued, as this was done by his father. The Appellant provided no additional response to the inquiry. The RAD finds the Appellant's testimony was evasive, as it did not address the question as put to him.

The RAD further finds that the Appellant's testimony regarding this issue undermines the genuineness of both documents, as the Appellant has not established how and when the documents were obtained. The RAD additionally notes that the RPD found the Appellant's testimony with respect to the RC document was not credible, and the document itself had significant concerns associated with its genuineness. It was assigned little weight in establishing the Appellant's identity. The RAD finds, after its review of the evidence, that there are sufficient unexplained credibility concerns with the Appellant's testimony about how and when he obtained these documents. The RAD supports the RPD's finding regarding this issue, and the Appellant's argument that the RPD dismissed the documents simply because the Appellant could not recall when he or his father obtained the documents must fail. The Lawyer's Letter and the Mother's Letters

The RPD found the letter from a lawyer in India20 and letters from the Appellant's mother21 were deserving of no evidentiary weight lacking in credibility in establishing the Appellant's personal identity or citizenship. The Appellant submits that the RPD rejected the lawyer's letter and letters from the Appellant's mother because the letters did not state what was expected. The RAD is not persuaded by the argument of the Appellant. The Lawyer's Letter

The RAD notes that the Appellant advances this argument but provides no additional evidence as to support their statement. The RAD has reviewed the lawyer's letter and notes the author states that the Appellant holds a Foreigner's Registration Certificate (RC) and a Green Book. The lawyer further states that he had confirmed the information that they had been given by the Foreigner's Registration office, although the author does not state what steps he took in order to verify that information. The RAD has previously identified credibility issues associated with these two documents and finds that the statements in the lawyer's letter are not capable of offsetting those concerns. Mother's Letter

The RAD has reviewed the initial letter in the form of an affidavit in the English language from the Appellant's mother in India and notes it provides no insight into the Appellant's personal circumstances surrounding his identity or country of citizenship. The RAD finds that there is no copy of the original letter in the mother's native language. The RAD notes that the record does not confirm that the Appellant's mother is fluent in reading and writing in the English language. A copy of a second letter in the form of an affidavit in the English language, dated September 21, 2017, does state that the Appellant was born on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in Tibet. The RAD finds the statements in the affidavit are insufficient to offset the negative credibility findings in the record.

The RAD notes that the affidavit is a statement of facts, but it is not an identity document. The RAD notes that the lack of identity documents is the central element of this appeal. The RAD agrees with the finding of the RPD that the letters are deserving of no evidentiary weight in establishing the Appellant's personal identity or country of citizenship. The Appellant's argument fails.

The RAD finds that, based on its analysis of all the evidence in the record, there is sufficient evidence to support the RPD's overall determination. The RAD finds that the Appellant has not established his personal identity, as per section 106 of the IRPA and Rule 11 of the RPD Rules, as a Tibetan-born individual who is stateless or that he is a citizen of the People's Republic of China. Having considered the lack of credible evidence regarding his identity documents, the RAD is not persuaded that there is a serious possibility that the Appellant would be persecuted in China on any Convention ground, nor that there exist substantial grounds to believe that the Appellant would be subjected personally to a danger of torture, nor is there a serious possibility that he will be subjected personally to a risk to his life or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in China.
The RAD finds that the Appellant has not established his identity.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD and dismisses the appeal.
